content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics, specifically focusing on rapid diagnostic methods for TB detection. This handbook, updated in 2021, provides detailed guidance on the implementation of WHO-recommended diagnostic tests and algorithms for TB and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). It is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-003058-9 and 978-92-4-003059-6. The publication is distributed under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If the work is translated, a disclaimer must be included, stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. Users are responsible for obtaining permissions for any third-party materials included in the work, such as tables, figures, or images, and for ensuring compliance with copyright laws. The handbook emphasizes the importance of rapid and accurate TB diagnosis, early detection of drug resistance, and prompt initiation of effective treatment regimens. It highlights the need for universal access to drug-susceptibility testing (DST) for all TB patients, particularly for rifampicin (RIF) resistance and, where applicable, for other drugs such as fluoroquinolones (FQs) and second-line injectable agents. WHO recommends phasing out injectable agents in favor of bedaquiline in treatment regimens, making rapid DST for amikacin unnecessary. The handbook outlines the steps and processes required to implement new diagnostic tools and provides model diagnostic algorithms incorporating the latest WHO recommendations. It also addresses practical considerations for scaling up laboratory capacity, including the use of molecular methods, liquid culture systems, electronic data systems, and diagnostic connectivity. Adherence to biosafety principles, quality assurance (QA) processes, and standard operating procedures (SOPs) is emphasized, along with the need for adequate human resources and funding. The WHO has introduced a class-based recommendation approach for diagnostic tools, focusing on groups of products with similar characteristics and performance rather than individual products. This approach aims to enhance competitiveness in price, quality, and services. Products are reviewed to determine whether they warrant a new class or fall under an existing class. If a new class is warranted, the product undergoes a first in class assessment through a Guideline Development Group (GDG) process. If it falls under an existing class, it is assessed by the WHO Prequalification (PQ) Unit to ensure quality and performance consistency. The handbook is intended for a wide audience, including ministry of health officials, donors, implementing partners, program managers, laboratory managers, clinicians, and other stakeholders involved in TB laboratory strengthening and program support. It provides references and links to original resources and is not meant to be a comprehensive manual but rather a practical guide for implementing WHO policies on TB diagnostics. The handbook also includes descriptions of WHO-reviewed technologies for TB and DR-TB detection, summarizes WHO recommendations for these technologies, and refers to relevant WHO policy statements. It highlights the importance of rapid diagnostic tests for detecting resistance to first-line and second-line drugs and the need for countries to expand their capacity to monitor culture conversion in patients undergoing treatment for DR-TB. The addition of a molecular test for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance in the latest guidelines is expected to facilitate testing for this drug.
